title: Swing Vote
full_review:
If you had any doubts about whether a visit to your local poll on Election Day really counts, the smartly made, consciousness-raising comedy "Swing Vote" (Touchstone) may help eradicate them.

 

Unabashedly formulaic but generally entertaining, the story concerns Bud Johnson (Kevin Costner), a beer-chugging, slovenly single father whose civically minded 12-year-old child, Molly (Madeline Carroll), runs their chaotic New Mexico trailer home.

Completely apathetic, Bud has zero interest in the upcoming presidential election -- with incumbent Republican Andrew Boone (Kelsey Grammer) facing off against Democratic rival Donald Greenleaf (Dennis Hopper) -- but Molly has taken it on herself to register him to vote.

 

On the appointed day, she's begged him to meet her at the voting place, but he lingers at his local watering hole, and ironically passes out after slamming into a "Vote Today" sign. The disappointed girl surreptitiously forges her dad's name in the register and attempts to vote on his behalf, with the volunteer attendant fast asleep, but a cleaning lady knocks off the power just as Molly's about to vote.

Bud and Molly are soon visited by some top state politicos who inform them that Bud's recast vote in 10 days' time will affect the state's five electoral votes, and therefore decide the next U.S. president.

They recommend Bud keep his identity secret, but it's not long before a resourceful local TV reporter, Kate Madison (Paula Patton), discovers the truth.

Both candidates and their respective campaign managers, Democrat Art Crumb (Nathan Lane) and Republican Martin Fox (Stanley Tucci), go to extravagant lengths to woo Bud, the former throwing a big bash at which Bud can resurrect his Willie Nelson knockoff band, and the latter offering a grand tour of Air Force One.

Comic complications ensue, with each candidate trying to take the stance of whatever ill-informed remark the clueless Bud happens to make. Throwing their own positions to the wind, Greenleaf and Boone take flip-flopping stands on everything from abortion to gay marriage to illegal immigration, as demonstrated by some satiric TV spots. The script plays it neutral on these topics, targeting the candidates themselves who are shamelessly willing to go to any lengths to win the popular vote.

Costner's terrific, and he and Carroll have good chemistry, though Bud's predictable reformation takes annoyingly long to happen. The script (co-written by Jason Richman and director Joshua Michael Stern) has Costner play the apathetic slob for virtually the entire film, and that includes multiple uses of the s-word and quite a bit of profanity.

Molly continually berates him for this, even telling him "You gotta stop using Jesus as a cuss word all the time."

Were it not for this gratuitously crass language, Bud's constant drinking and a sordid domestic incident near the end, the film could be warmly recommended to all ages

But those caveats aside, the overriding messages -- the importance of every vote and the integrity of the political process -- are painlessly delivered, with the script wisely taking a nonpartisan position.

The film contains much crude language, profanity and crass expressions; heavy drinking; brief irreverence; and some domestic discord. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
